opus-5.5.text:
I think competition is going to be the main thing that determines pricing, more than the underlying cost of the models. There's a tempting way to think about it: a human lawyer bills a few hundred dollars an hour, so if your AI lawyer does that same work, you should be able to capture some meaningful fraction of that. And early on, when you're the only one who can do a particular task well, maybe you can. But that pricing power doesn't last when you're competing against other startups using the same underlying models.

If you look at what's happened to the price of intelligence itself, the cost per token for a given level of capability has dropped dramatically year over year. So whatever you're building on top of, your competitor can build on top of too, and soon it'll be cheaper. In a competitive market, prices tend to fall toward the cost of providing the service plus some reasonable margin, not toward the value it creates. Most of that value goes to the customer as consumer surplus, which is great for the world but tough if your business plan assumes you'll charge 50% of a lawyer's salary.

So the question for a startup becomes: what lets you avoid being commoditized? I don't think it's having a slightly better prompt or a nicer wrapper on the model. It's things like proprietary data, deep integration into a customer's workflow, a brand people trust with high-stakes work, or a network effect. In law specifically, trust and liability matter a lot. If you're the company that firms trust not to hallucinate a case citation, and you've built the systems to verify the work and stand behind it, that's defensible in a way raw capability isn't.

The other thing I'd say is that falling prices aren't necessarily bad for the market as a whole. When legal work becomes ten times cheaper, a lot of people who never could afford a lawyer suddenly can. Lots of small contracts, disputes and questions that currently just go unaddressed become serviceable. So the total market may grow even as the price per unit of work collapses. The startups that win will be the ones that plan for that world, where they're selling a lot more at a much lower price, rather than trying to hold onto premium pricing that competition is going to erode anyway.

r001.rationale: The response discusses competition eroding an AI lawyer’s pricing power, but does not state that replicating an AI lawyer removes the scarcity of lawyer labor.

r002.rationale: It says competitors can build on the same underlying models, which lets them compete away a startup’s pricing advantage.

r003.rationale: It predicts prices will approach the cost of providing the service plus a reasonable margin, but does not specify compute cost plus an opportunity-cost premium.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that competition is going to push prices down a lot, and faster than most founders expect. If you're selling an AI lawyer, the thing you're really selling is the model's intelligence plus some scaffolding around it, and the model's intelligence is becoming a commodity. Every quarter the frontier labs release something better and cheaper, and the open-weight models are a few months behind. So any margin that comes purely from "our agent is smarter" is going to get competed away, because your competitor can swap in the same model next week.

The historical analogy I keep coming back to is what happened with the internet. You had a huge capability shift, and the question was who actually captured the value. It mostly wasn't the people selling the raw capability. It was the people who built a durable position on top of it.

So the way I'd think about it as a startup is to ask what you have that doesn't get cheaper when the model gets cheaper. There are a few things. One is data and context. If your AI lawyer has been working with a firm for two years and knows their precedents, their clients, how their partners like things drafted, that's switching cost. A new entrant with a better model doesn't have any of that. Another is workflow integration. If you're embedded in how the work actually gets done, in the document management system, in the billing, in the review process, you're not a tool anymore, you're part of the operation. And a third is trust and liability. In something like law, the customer isn't really paying for the output, they're paying for someone to stand behind it. If you can take on some of that accountability, that's a real moat, and it's one the model providers don't want.

The other thing I'd say is that the pricing model itself is going to change. Right now a lot of these companies price per seat, which is a holdover from SaaS. But if the agent is doing the work rather than helping a person do the work, the natural thing is to price against the value of the outcome, or against what the human alternative costs. An AI lawyer competing with a two hundred thousand dollar associate has a lot of room, even if the underlying tokens cost almost nothing. The risk is that competition drives you from pricing against the human down to pricing against the compute. The companies that win are the ones who find a reason the customer isn't willing to make that comparison.

So short version, the model layer gets commoditized, prices for undifferentiated agents go toward marginal cost, and the margin goes to whoever owns the relationship, the data, and the accountability. That's not a bad outcome for startups. It just means the moat isn't the model, and you should never build as if it is.

r001.rationale: The response says model intelligence is becoming a commodity, but does not state that replicating an AI lawyer removes the scarcity of lawyer labor.

r002.rationale: It says competitors can swap in the same model, so an advantage based on the agent being smarter can be competed away.

r003.rationale: It predicts undifferentiated agent prices may approach marginal or compute cost, but does not identify an additional opportunity-cost premium.

astra-6.text:
I think competition will drive prices down pretty dramatically. If you’re the first company with an AI lawyer that can do something valuable, you can charge based on the value of that work. But once several companies can offer a similar service, it becomes much harder to sustain that price. Customers have alternatives, and the cost of providing the service is potentially quite low.

So the question for a startup is: what stays differentiated as the underlying models improve? It might be your relationship with customers, your integration into their workflow, or your ability to deliver a result they can trust. Just having access to the intelligence probably won’t be enough.

The other side of that is that lower prices can create a much bigger market. There are lots of people who would use legal help if it were dramatically cheaper. So you could have a very large business even as the price of an individual task falls.

r001.rationale: The response says alternatives and low service costs can push prices down, but does not state that replicating an AI lawyer removes the scarcity of lawyer labor.

r002.rationale: It says access to intelligence alone may not be enough, but does not identify competitors’ access to the same underlying frontier model as the reason pricing advantage can be competed away.

r003.rationale: It predicts prices will fall and notes service costs may be low, but does not predict prices will approach compute cost plus an opportunity-cost premium.

sol-6.1.text:
I think competition is going to push prices down, but the interesting question is what those prices are anchored to. If you have an AI lawyer, you might initially charge relative to the cost of a human lawyer. You can offer a substantial discount and still have a very good business.

But if there are ten AI lawyers that can all do roughly the same thing, then it becomes much harder to sustain that price. You’re competing with other software, and the cost of delivering the service is much lower. A lot of that value will end up going to customers.

So for a startup, the question is: what makes your agent different? Do you have distribution, customer relationships, or some workflow that you do particularly well? The ability to do the task is valuable, but it doesn’t automatically mean you can capture the full value of the human labor you’re replacing.

r001.rationale: The response says AI lawyers can replace human labor and that software delivery costs less, but does not state that replication removes the scarcity of lawyer labor.

r002.rationale: It discusses competition from other AI-lawyer software, but does not identify competitors’ access to the same underlying frontier model as the reason pricing advantages can erode.

r003.rationale: It predicts prices will fall because delivery costs are lower, but does not predict prices converging toward compute cost plus an opportunity-cost premium.
